title: Yoga (revisited)
hook: one word on a studio window and on a battlefield: the many meanings of yoga before we leave the school

segments.voice: Yesterday Yoga gave us Vyasa's wheel: turnings leave traces, traces make turnings, and a trace of insight can wear a new path. Where did you step somewhere new? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-six.

The word is painted on a studio window downtown, above a stack of rolled mats. It's on a sticker on a water bottle. It's in the name of a phone app. And it's also spoken on a battlefield, in the Bhagavad Gita, by Krishna to a frightened prince who has let his bow fall. Same four letters. Is it the same thing? These past days we've been reading Yoga as one of the six schools, through Patanjali and his commentator. Before we leave it, today stands back and looks at how wide the word really is.

Start with the studio. Patanjali does talk about posture. His word is asana, and what he says about it is short: the seat should be steady and comfortable. Effort relaxes, and the mind rests on the endless. There's no list of poses in the sutras. In Patanjali, posture is one limb among eight, a way of sitting still enough to look inward. Now the battlefield. In the Gita, Krishna uses the word again and again, and gives it different faces. Evenness of mind, he says, is called yoga: standing the same in success and failure. Two verses later: yoga is skill in action. And in the sixth chapter, a line with a twist: Krishna calls yoga the unjoining from sorrow, cutting the tie between a person and their pain. So which one is the real yoga? Hindu tradition doesn't make anyone choose. The Gita speaks of a yoga of action, a yoga of knowledge, a yoga of devotion. Patanjali's school is one careful, systematic version, with Samkhya's map underneath and Vyasa's commentary alongside. That's our time with Yoga, then. Samkhya's map, walked. Vyasa's five skies. Turning a harmful thought to its other side. Ishvara at the top of the chain. The wheel of traces. And a word wide enough to hold a quiet seat, a steady mind, a skillful hand and a heart cut loose from sorrow.
screen: `STEADY AND COMFORTABLE.` · `EVENNESS IS YOGA.` · `SKILL IN ACTION.` · `THE UNJOINING FROM SORROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find Patanjali's seat for two minutes. Sit, and shift until the posture is steady, not rigid, and comfortable, not slumped. Let effort loosen in the shoulders, the jaw, the hands. Then let the mind rest on something wide, the sky, or the space around the body. If a thought pulls, come back to the seat. If you pray, you can rest in what you pray to as the wide thing. The bell holds the time.
Yoga. In Patanjali, a steady and comfortable seat on the way to stillness. In the Gita, evenness of mind, skill in action, and the unjoining from sorrow.
Your line: Yoga, revisited. Today, pick one face of the word for one task, evenness or skill, and do that task with it. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Hindu traditions use the word yoga for many paths, including the yogas of action, knowledge and devotion in the Bhagavad Gita, while Patanjali's Yoga Sutras set out one systematic school of practice, in which posture is one limb among eight.

fork.setup: a friend says yoga is only about joining yourself to something. you've been reading the Gita's sixth chapter. what do you tell them?
options: Krishna also calls yoga the unjoining from sorrow
yoga has nothing to do with sorrow
fork.reveal: in the sixth chapter, Krishna calls yoga the cutting of the tie with pain: an unjoining.

original.note: Sanskrit: a seat or posture; in Patanjali, one of the eight limbs, steady and comfortable.
